extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, improv teachers, troupe leaders, and festival programmers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for performing, teaching, directing, and programming improvisational comedy (short- and long-form), emphasizing listening, group play, pedagogy, innovation, and audience relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Help the other person / give the other improviser what they want
rubrics_metrics.description: Help the other person; try and give the other improviser what they want.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fundamental job in improv is to help your partner succeed. Look to supply offers that support their choices rather than obstructing them; this builds scenes and group-mind cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be obvious; don't try to be clever
rubrics_metrics.description: Also don't try to be clever. Be obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid forcing cleverness — obvious choices are clearer for partners and audience, and create stronger material. Trying to be clever often derails scenes and reduces connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be audible
rubrics_metrics.description: Be audible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear projection and diction are basic performance requirements so offers are heard and can be built on. Poor audibility weakens the scene and frustrates partners and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen (above all else)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trust your partner, the audience is already on your side, and above all else . . . listen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listening is repeatedly emphasized as the single most important skill; it enables agreement, discovery, callbacks, and truthful responses. Lack of listening is a primary cause of poor improv.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust and generosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Trust your partner; be generous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trusting partners and generous play (giving status, space, and support) create an accepting room where scenes can develop. Generosity also includes not 'pimping' guests unless you know them and the right spirit of playful teasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be humble and courageous; fear shows as arrogance
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear—which often comes across as arrogance. We want improvisers to look humble and courageous. Your job is to sell good nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performers should appear confident but humble; fear makes people act defensively. 'Selling good nature' means projecting openness rather than defensiveness or showmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek truthfulness over forced funniness
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be nice if people were interested in being truthful rather than funny. Because truthful things are funnier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize truthful, specific choices and emotional honesty — comedy arises from truth. Avoid prioritizing jokes over authentic scene work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play at the top of your intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Play at the top of your intelligence. The humor comes out of that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring real intelligence to choices; don't play down to the audience. Humor comes from connections, callbacks, and layered information — like attentive chess play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement is with the actor not the character
rubrics_metrics.description: The agreement is not with the character, it’s with the actor. The agreement is not 'Sure you can rob me, take everything.' That’s not agreeing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agreeing should support scene reality while preserving dramatic tension. Blindly accepting character actions at the expense of conflict destroys drama; instead, accept offers while keeping integrity and stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use callbacks, recycling, and connections to build laughs
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowing that the humor comes from the connections, the callbacks, the recycling of the information that your partner used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Returning to earlier bits, weaving callbacks and recycled information increases energy and comedic payoff; remembering and reusing details deepens scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: If stuck, silence or repetition can be funnier than forcing lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Not knowing what to say—saying nothing or repeating what someone else has said is always funnier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When unsure, simpler responses (silence, repetition) can heighten awkwardness and comedic tension; avoid filling space with desperate 'clever' lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public work should at least match rehearsal quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless your work in public is better than your work in rehearsals, there’s something seriously wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rehearsal should be the testing and refining ground; if live shows are weaker, address process and preparation. Strive for rehearsal rigor that translates to performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach with a lesson plan but stay flexible
rubrics_metrics.description: Having a lesson plan, but always being willing to toss it out the window in favor of what’s happening in the room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good teachers prepare structured progressions but respond to student needs and emergent learning moments; balance curriculum with situational responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set up exercises that help students teach themselves; teach with a beginner’s mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Set up the exercises to aid the students in teaching themselves, serving more as experienced guide than expert. Teach with a beginner’s mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design drills that encourage discovery and peer learning. Adopt curiosity and openness so students feel empowered to experiment and internalize principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a point of view and credit sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Having a point of view is important. It gives something for the students to either agree or disagree with... It is important to know and give credit to where exercises and ideas come from.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articulate your methodology so students can position themselves; acknowledge influences (Spolin, Johnstone, Close) to contextualize exercises and avoid dogmatism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and innovation: mix schools and avoid dogmatic camps
rubrics_metrics.description: Improv should be inclusive, not exclusive... everyone was talking about the same thing but with a different emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage cross-pollination of Del Close, Keith Johnstone, Spolin and other approaches. Avoid rigid camp divisions; experiment and adapt methods to goals (storytelling, game play, theatricality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Address plateaus by changing routines and maintaining persistence
rubrics_metrics.description: When plateauing: try things differently—change up your game choices, your warm-ups, your characters, the clothes to perform in, the route to the theatre ... keep improvising through it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plateaus are normal; remedy them by deliberate variation and sustained practice rather than avoidance. Viewing plateaus as a creative rebirth helps artists progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be inclusive and reflect society in casting and workshops
rubrics_metrics.description: We need to make our workshops more accessible and welcoming to different sectors of society... if we are to reflect society in any meaningful comedic way, we need to reflect the views and values of that society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively recruit and adapt pedagogy to diverse participants so improv represents broader perspectives; diversification is both ethical and artistically necessary for relevant comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Festival/program selection: look for teams that show another way and overall excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: We always look for groups that can show us another way of creating, playing and performing improv... ensembles who demonstrate overall excellence in what they do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programmers should prioritize originality, demonstrable craft, and international or stylistic diversity; teams that expand the vocabulary of improv or exemplify high skill are favored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid copied forms without understanding; teach full instructions and philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Misunderstanding games, concepts, philosophies... many times improvisers doing or teaching things without all the instructions or understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because improv is an oral craft, ensure teachers transmit not just exercises but their intent and philosophy. Prevent degradation via partial or decontextualized teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design apprenticeship and outreach to develop new talent
rubrics_metrics.description: Apprentice program: private coaching, free tickets to see shows, artistic and business consultation and a chance to perform as guided by their private coach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mentorship, coaching and performance opportunities to cultivate ensembles. Institutional support (not-for-profit status, teen/college programs) helps sustain the art form and pipeline of performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use space, ensemble familiarity, and callbacks as structural strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: The Store is like a sitcom with six people who know each other very well... we have so many callbacks. Some guest players change the way you improvise (use whole space, go into audience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage tight ensemble rapport, physical staging, and recurring motifs/callbacks to create a coherent, high-energy show. Be aware that guest dynamics can expand or alter company patterns.
